title: OBJECTIVE REALITY AND CONSCIOUSNESS
excerpt: How much of the world do we encounter, and how much do we bring to it?
quote: "Reality is created by our mind, we can change our reality by changing our mind." - Plato
body:
There is something peculiar about being conscious: it is the condition through which we experience everything, yet it remains extraordinarily difficult to explain. What does it mean to be aware—to feel time passing, recognise your reflection, or hear your own thoughts? Is consciousness something we direct, or something we find ourselves possessing, as indispensable and involuntary as a heartbeat? We can choose to concentrate, but we do not seem to choose the existence of the awareness due to which that concentration occurs.

Before we ask whether we see reality clearly, perhaps we must ask what it means to be the one seeing. Objective reality, as I mean it here, is the world as it exists independently of anyone’s perception of it. Subjective reality is how that world appears from within a particular life. A clock measures the minutes of a lecture and an examination with equal indifference. Yet one hour can at times feel interminable, while also seeming to disappear before you have finished the last question. The interval may be the same but the experience is profoundly different.

This distinction becomes more unsettling when we turn from time to other people. Have you ever entertained the thought that life resembles a simulated game, with you at its centre and everyone else appearing as a character whose inner world remains inaccessible? As a thought experiment, it exposes an asymmetry we ordinarily overlook: you experience your own consciousness directly, while encountering everyone else’s through their actions and words alone. Your thoughts arrive with an intimacy that another person’s never can. You feel your own grief but you witness someone else’s tears. You know the effort behind your decisions while you see only fragments of the deliberation behind theirs.

So how can you know for sure if others do indeed posses and brain and aren't placeholder characters of the simulation you're in. The important thing to remember is that absence of direct access is not evidence of the absence of the conscious mind of others. They speak of memories, apprehensions, desires, and contradictions much like your own. Their lives display the same complexity that you recognise from within. To accept that they are conscious is to recognise that your privileged access to yourself does not make you uniquely real since from their perspective, you are the person whose interior life cannot be seen.

There is an ethical consequence to this recognition. Every stranger you pass may experience their existence with the same immediacy with which you experience yours. They have concerns that occupy them completely, memories you will never inherit, and private meanings attached to places you would walk past without noticing. Your perspective is the centre of your experience; it need not be the centre of all existence even though that is not how we perceive our reality, our subjective reality.

Even the way I just described the brain suggest something baffling. It implies that your brain is separate from you and it can observe you the way it does others. When you look into a mirror, think about thinking about yourself, the apparent distinction can feel very convincing. Yet this ability of the brain does not, by itself, establish a you separate from your consciousness. Perhaps this recursive awareness is part of what the mind does to give you the superpower of self reflection. A stronger assertion I make that “you are your brain” is a philosophical position, rather than a conclusion this feeling alone can settle.

Hence the question of reality becomes more subtle. Consciousness and command are not synonymous. A thought can appear uninvited; a feeling can arrive before we understand its cause. We may be able to examine, redirect, or act upon what arises without having chosen its arrival. Our notion of reality, dictated by consciousness is therefore not commandeered by us, or is it?

title: THE SAND RECKONER
excerpt: The universe isn't infinite, our tools just weren't big enough to count it.
body:
In his treatise The Sand Reckoner, Archimedes confronts a seemingly insurmountable question: how many grains of sand would it take to fill the universe?

At a time when Greek numerical system was ill-equipped to express quantities of extraordinary magnitude, Archimedes devised a mathematical framework that extended numerical thought far beyond its conventional limits. His objective was not to find a finite number or to count the uncountable, but to refute the prevailing notion that quantities on such an immense scale were inherently inexpressible. He sought to demonstrate that even the seemingly infinite could be approached through the disciplined language of mathematics.

By estimating the universe's diameter at no more than $10^{14}$ stadia, Archimedes calculated that filling it with sand would require a quantity equivalent to approximately $8 \times 10^{63}$ grains in modern notation, a figure far below the upper limits of his newly created system, what in modern day is referred to as the place value notation.

Archimedes demonstrated that the boundaries of knowledge are often determined less by the scale of a problem and rather the limitations of the tools with which we approach it. This leaves us with the question: If the universe can be rendered intelligible through mathematics, did he construct the most powerful framework through which the human mind can comprehend it?

title: THE ENIGMA OF CONSCIOUSNESS
excerpt: What if the boundary between your mind and the universe is merely an illusion of perspective?
quote: "Consciousness is a singular of which the plural is unknown"
body:
Erwin Schrödinger’s aphorism intimates one of the most profound enigma's of existence: whether consciousness, despite its apparent multiplicity, is fundamentally one rather than a collection of separate, self-contained experiences.

If consciousness cannot be meaningfully pluralized, then the distinction between the observer and the observed, between you and I, may be far less fundamental than our subjective experience suggests. If consciousness is singular, are we truly separate beings experiencing the universe, or is it the universe experiencing itself through us?

Just as waves are the ocean’s way of expressing movement, in a similar sense our individual consciousnesses (plural) are like a ripple in the universal mind or conscious (singular). The daily impression of separate minds may simply be this single conscious reality looking back at itself through different pairs of eyes.

While this perspective remains a philosophical interpretation rather than a scientific conclusion, it compels us to reconsider our most basic assumption of existence, inviting us to see beyond the illusion of division.
